chunks: "My approach is always the same. First I check there's negative feedback, meaning the output goes back to the inverting input.
If so, the op-amp is going to work to keep the two inputs at the same voltage, and the inputs draw essentially no current. Then it's just KCL.
Take the inverting amplifier, input resistor R1, feedback resistor Rf, and the plus input grounded.
The minus input is a virtual ground at 0 volts, so the current in is Vin over R1.
None of it can go into the op-amp, so all of it flows through Rf, which drops Vin times Rf over R1 and the output sits at minus that. So gain is minus Rf over R1.
For the non-inverting one, the minus input is held at Vin, and Rf and R1 form a divider from the output, so Vin equals Vout times R1 over R1 plus Rf, giving gain 1 plus Rf over R1.
A buffer is the special case with gain of one. The same trick gives the summing amp, difference amp, and with a capacitor in the feedback path, an integrator.

Then I'd mention the real limits: the output can't go past the rails, the closed-loop bandwidth is the gain-bandwidth product divided by the gain, and the slew rate limits large high-frequency signals."
